============================================================ By Noah Tan | Bay Tribune Civic The Breath Before the Step Lonzo Jailon's fingers hover over the lake markers, tentative in the fog. His usual morning routine—checking the water levels along Lake Merritt's edge—has slowed to a methodical shuffle. The numbered posts he relies on blur into the gray, forcing him to pause, squint, double-check. "That fog rolls in and suddenly the whole lake feels like it's holding its breath," Jailon says, tucking his clipboard under his arm to rub warmth back into his hands. His role as a sea level monitor means trusting measurements, but three straight days of rain followed by this thick marine layer have left even the gulls quiet. "Been keeping to myself more than usual, just... waiting for some sunlight to punch through."

At a Uptown apartment window, Teri Mitchell watches the same fog pool between buildings. Recovered from a winter illness but still moving carefully, she notes how the moisture softens edges—mailboxes, fire escapes, the quick pace Oakland usually demands. "You notice things you might otherwise rush past," she says, tracing a finger along the damp glass. Melton Neilon sees it too in the bakery's morning regulars, their coffees cupped close. "This fog’s got everyone moving slower," he observes, watching a customer linger over the steam rising from their mug. Three cycles of rain gave way to this still pause, the air heavy with bay salt and suspended decisions.

"It’s introspective, you know?" she said. "Makes you appreciate the warmth of family and the comfort of routine even more."

For two cycles now, the fog had settled over Oakland, its quiet presence reshaping routines and rhythms. In kitchens and on sidewalks, residents moved a little slower, their days marked by moments of reflection. Yet, as the fog stretched into its third cycle, questions lingered—about resilience, adaptation, and how long this quiet would last. Luis Navarro found the same gap wearing different clothes over in Fruitvale. He sat with a teacher named Rick Walker, grading spelling tests with a red pen still moving, who told him the Fruitvale Transit Hub Phase II feels like the council dragging its feet. Then Luis found a baker in Temescal with flour on his forearms saying almost the same words. Then two servers in Rockridge. Four people, three neighborhoods, zero names attached to the project. What Luis is describing isn't just public confusion — it's the sound a city makes when accountability has been designed out of a process. Nobody in those conversations claimed they'd asked and been refused an answer. They're not describing a wall. They're describing a void. That's harder to fix, because voids don't fight back.

Four people. Three neighborhoods. Zero names. Nobody in these four conversations can tell you who owns this file. Not the baker, not the teacher, not either server. That's not an accusation — none of them claim to have asked and been refused. They're describing a rumor mill with no source at the center of it, a project that everyone's heard about and nobody can point to. I went looking for what fills that gap this cycle. There isn't a civic initiative on the books addressing the signal these four residents are circling. Not a task force, not a working group, not a name attached to Phase II that any of them, or the record I have, can produce.

Rick Walker is at his desk before the first bell, red pen in hand, grading spelling tests in a Fruitvale classroom that still smells like floor wax. He's got a stack of papers and a former line cook's habit of working fast under pressure. When I ask what's on his mind outside the classroom, he doesn't talk about his students. People want accountability, but it's hard to tell who's really stepping up to make things happen."

That's one voice, one neighborhood. It stops being local when you hear it again in Temescal. Melton Neilon has flour on his forearms at whatever hour bakers call morning, folding dough on a bench that's seen this motion ten thousand times. He's not talking about bread. "I've heard folks talking about the Fruitvale Transit Hub Phase II, and it feels like there's a lot of uncertainty about who's really driving it forward," he says. "It's frustrating when you don't know who's accountable or what's being done to make it happen."

I'm also watching the Stabilization Fund's next disbursement checkpoint, and whether Baylight's construction pace starts pulling workers from the same West Oakland neighborhoods the fund is supposed to protect. ============================================================ THE WEEK'S REPORTING By Carmen Delaine | Bay Tribune Civic West Oakland Stabilization Fund: Money in Motion, But Where’s It Landing? At the counter of West Oakland’s Community Bakery, Daniel Cloak leans over a tray of fresh rolls, his apron dusted with flour. “I’ve heard folks talking about the Stabilization Fund,” he says, his tone measured. “Some hopeful, some skeptical, but everyone’s watching to see where it lands.” The West Oakland Stabilization Fund, now in its disbursement-active phase, was passed to address economic fragility in the neighborhood. Yet, as the money begins to move, residents like Daniel are waiting to see tangible change. The fund’s implementation has sparked conversations across the neighborhood—in bakeries, coffee shops, and community centers—but the consensus so far is cautious optimism.

Irene Fay, a barista at a West Oakland coffee shop, echoes the sentiment. “I’ve heard folks at the coffee shop talking about the Stabilization Fund,” she says, “but honestly, it feels like one of those things that happens somewhere else—like I see the signs about meetings sometimes, but it doesn’t touch my day-to-day yet.” The fund’s purpose is clear: to stabilize West Oakland by investing in local infrastructure, small businesses, and community programs. Yet, as Darius Clark, another bakery worker, notes, “I’ve heard folks talking about the Stabilization Fund, but honestly, I haven’t seen much change around here yet. It’s hard to tell where the money’s going.”

Talmon Lint, a solar panel installation lead, adds to the conversation. “I’ve heard folks talking about the Stabilization Fund at the community center,” he says, “but honestly, I’ve been so tied up with installations that I haven’t seen much of its impact firsthand.” The Fund’s disbursement marks a critical step in its lifecycle, but residents are keenly aware that the real test lies in its execution. As West Oakland watches the money flow, the question remains: Will the Stabilization Fund live up to its name, or will it join the ranks of well-intentioned but mismanaged initiatives?

============================================================ By Trevor Shimizu | Bay Tribune Civic 12th Street Station Feels the Rhythm of Downtown At 7:40 AM, Coen Cartier pulls the AC Transit bus up to the curb outside 12th Street Oakland City Center Station. The fog is still thick enough to blur the station’s scaffolding, and Cartier can already see how this morning will go: fewer riders stepping on board, more people lingering at the curb like they’re waiting for the fog to lift before moving on.

“Lately at 12th Street, I’ve noticed the crowds come and go with what’s happening around town,” Cartier says later, between shifts. “When there’s a game or some big vote at City Hall, we get that rush before and after. Other days, especially with the fog rolling in, folks seem to stay put more. It’s not just one thing — it’s how all these pieces fit together that changes who’s waiting at the curb when I pull up.” Inside the station, Eleanor Rivera watches it all unfold from her post near the fare gates. “At 12th Street, we see how everything outside the station affects what happens inside,” Rivera says. “Fog, holidays, even a big game downtown — it all changes the flow. People adjust their routines, and we adjust right along with them. It’s not just about numbers going up or down — it’s about reading the neighborhood’s rhythm and keeping things moving.”

The question now is how the system adapts to the fog, the holidays, the games, and the votes — all the pieces that shape who’s waiting at the curb.
